---
title: "Python answer tests"
subtitle: "Basis questions, matrix properties, and your own checker"
---

STACK SymPy can grade a family of correct answers without comparing each entry
to one model answer. The built-in `IsBasis` and `MatrixProperty` tests cover
common matrix tasks; `PythonChecker` lets an author define another predicate.
All three use the usual STACK response-tree (PRT) branches for scores and
feedback. The Python predicate decides whether a response meets the condition;
it does not assign marks by itself. Try the [matrix and custom-checker
questions](../examples.qmd#find-a-nonidentity-matrix-with-determinant-one).

## Choose the mathematical test

| Task | Test | What it accepts |
|---|---|---|
| Give this particular matrix | `AlgEquiv` | Equal dimensions and equivalent corresponding entries. This is a native STACK answer-test name. |
| Give any basis of a matrix's null, column, or row space | `IsBasis` | Any independent family spanning the requested space. |
| Give any basis of a space specified by basis vectors | `IsBasis` | Any independent family with the same span as those vectors. |
| Give a matrix satisfying one of the built-in conditions | `MatrixProperty` | Exact integer-entry, determinant, or identity checks. Separate PRTs can award marks for separate requirements. |
| Give a matrix satisfying another condition, such as positive definiteness | `PythonChecker` | A named function in a selected author file decides the condition. |

The three Python tests are extensions of this port. A STACK XML file that uses
them still has familiar inputs and PRTs, but importing it into Moodle does not
install those tests. A native STACK version needs equivalent Maxima checks and,
for a resizable input, native input configuration. The existing native answer
tests keep their meaning; these examples do not count as native compatibility
results.

## Basis questions: use the matrix in the question

For a null-space question about $A$, place the original matrix in the PRT's
teacher answer (`tans`) and select `nullspace`. Similarly select `columnspace`
or `rowspace` for those spaces. The learner enters one proposed vector per
column for `nullspace` and `columnspace`, or per row for `rowspace`:

```xml
<answertest>IsBasis</answertest>
<sans>ans</sans>
<tans>A</tans>
<testoptions>nullspace</testoptions>
```

Here `A` is a question variable holding the **original matrix**, not a
precomputed null-space basis. Set the input's model answer with
`<tans>nullspace_basis(A)</tans>`; corresponding helpers are
`columnspace_basis(A)` and `rowspace_basis(A)`. These author-side helpers
provide a model response; the test still accepts any valid basis. A nonzero
rescaling, reordered vectors, or a different independent combination can all
be correct. For example, if
$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{pmatrix}$, both the columns of
$\begin{pmatrix}-2&-3\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and the columns of
$\begin{pmatrix}-5&-1\\1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ form bases of $\ker A$.

The older `columns` and `rows` options instead take a known, independent basis
in the PRT's `tans` and compare the learner's span with that reference span.
Choose these only when the question defines its target by a reference basis.
A reference that spans the wrong space would define the wrong answer.

| `IsBasis` option | PRT `tans` means | Submitted vectors |
|---|---|---|
| `nullspace` | Original matrix $A$ | Columns spanning $\ker A$ |
| `columnspace` | Original matrix $A$ | Columns spanning $\operatorname{col}(A)$ |
| `rowspace` | Original matrix $A$ | Rows spanning $\operatorname{row}(A)$ |
| `columns` (also the default) | Independent reference columns | Columns with the same span |
| `rows` | Independent reference rows | Rows with the same span |

The matrix options use exact rational entries (integers and fractions), not
decimals or symbolic parameters. Inputs have 1–16 rows or columns and at most
64 entries. The editor cannot represent the empty basis of a zero-dimensional
space, so avoid a target space with dimension zero. Give the learner enough
room to choose the required number of vectors; [matrix input](matrix-input.qmd)
explains bounded resizing. Test an alternative correct basis, an incomplete
family, a dependent family, and a vector outside the target space with qtests.
The input's model answer is checked at build time against the PRT; a mismatched
model or dimensions stop the build.

The response tree awards the marks on its true and false branches. Basis
questions here award full credit only for a complete basis. After checking,
green marks a valid vector in an independent submitted family, yellow marks
members of a dependent valid family, and red marks zero or out-of-space
vectors. Green can therefore appear on an incomplete answer. The colors are
diagnostics, not partial marks. Editing or resizing clears them and requires
validation again.

## Matrix conditions and partial credit

The [determinant-one example](../examples.qmd#find-a-nonidentity-matrix-with-determinant-one)
asks for an integer $2\times2$ matrix with determinant $1$, other than the
identity. It uses three equally weighted PRTs, one per condition. A response
meeting two conditions earns two thirds of the available marks. An entry-by-entry
comparison with one model matrix would miss other correct answers.

| `MatrixProperty` option | Teacher answer in `tans` | Question checked |
|---|---|---|
| `integer_entries` | `true` or `false` | Are all entries integers? |
| `determinant` | Exact rational value, such as `1` | Does a square matrix have this determinant? |
| `identity` | `true` or `false` | Is this the identity matrix? |

All submitted entries must be exact rationals for this built-in test. Set true and false branch
scores and feedback for each PRT explicitly; the editor does not infer
per-cell marks. The model answer must satisfy the authored nodes. In these
nodes, `tans` is the expected **result of the property**: `1` for determinant,
`true` to require integer entries, and `false` to exclude the identity. It is
not the original matrix from the question. These three option names are the
complete built-in `MatrixProperty` vocabulary; for another matrix condition,
write a `PythonChecker` function.

For example, a node asking for determinant $1$ has `<tans>1</tans>` and
`<testoptions>determinant</testoptions>`. The learner's matrix is named in
`<sans>ansm</sans>`; the model matrix belongs to the **input's** `tans`.

## Symmetric positive definite matrices {#symmetric-positive-definite-matrices}

Suppose learners must give **any symmetric positive definite $2\times2$
matrix** with integer or exact-fraction entries. `AlgEquiv` would compare
entries with one model answer. `MatrixProperty` has no positive-definiteness
option. A small `PythonChecker` function can express this mathematical rule:
for a real symmetric matrix, Sylvester's criterion requires every leading
principal determinant to be positive. For
$\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}$, that means $a>0$ and $ac-b^2>0$.

### 1. Save the checker file

Save this complete code as [`questions/spd-checker.py`](../questions/spd-checker.py).
The `CHECKERS` dictionary makes `is_spd` available by name:

```python
"""Check symmetric positive definiteness for exact rational matrices."""


def is_spd(ansm, expected):
    if any(entry.is_Rational is not True for entry in ansm):
        return {"valid": False, "correct": False,
                "feedback": "Use integers or exact fractions in every cell."}

    if ansm.rows != ansm.cols or ansm != ansm.T:
        positive = False
    else:
        # Sylvester's criterion for real symmetric matrices.
        positive = all(ansm[:k, :k].det() > 0 for k in range(1, ansm.rows + 1))

    correct = bool(positive) == bool(expected)
    return {"valid": True, "correct": correct,
            "feedback": "" if correct else
                "The matrix must be symmetric, with every leading principal determinant positive."}


CHECKERS = {"is_spd": is_spd}
```

The function receives the parsed learner matrix as `ansm` and the expected
property result as `expected`. An entry outside the exact-rational domain
produces an invalid-input message. A well-formed matrix that is not SPD
returns `valid=True, correct=False` for this exercise and follows the PRT's
false branch. A plain `True` or `False` would also work if no diagnostic is
needed.

### 2. Connect it to the question XML

In the [complete question XML](../questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml),
the matrix input `ansm` uses `<tans>matrix([1,0],[0,1])</tans>` as a model
answer. This fixes the editor at $2\times2$; the identity is **one** accepted
answer, not the only one. The response-tree node selects the learner matrix,
passes the desired property value, and awards marks on its normal branches:

```xml
<answertest>PythonChecker</answertest>
<sans>ansm</sans>
<tans>true</tans>
<testoptions>is_spd</testoptions>
<truescoremode>=</truescoremode><truescore>1</truescore>
<falsescoremode>=</falsescoremode><falsescore>0</falsescore>
```

Here `tans` means **the checker should find SPD to be true**. It is a
parameter passed to the custom function, not automatically the original
matrix in the prompt. The XML's seven author tests include another correct
integer matrix, a fractional correct matrix, and negative definite,
semidefinite, nonsymmetric and indefinite examples. The checker decides
`correct`; the PRT alone awards credit and gives authored branch feedback.

### 3. Add the question to a Quarto page

Use just the checker **filename** alongside the XML file and question name:

```{.stack-question #docs-spd-matrix}
#| file: ../questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml
#| question: A symmetric positive definite matrix
#| python-checkers: ../questions/spd-checker.py
#| review: true
```

This live card and the [examples page](../examples.qmd#symmetric-positive-definite-matrix)
use the same files. Paths are relative to this `.qmd` page; a root-level page
uses `questions/...`. Quarto reads the Python file at build time and includes
its contents for the browser checker. The author supplies only that filename.
The XML names `is_spd` but contains no Python source or file path.

### 4. Run the author tests

From the project root, run:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=_extensions/stack-sympy python -m stack_sympy.cli test \
  --file questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml \
  --python-checkers questions/spd-checker.py
quarto render
```

Then try a different correct response such as `matrix([2,1],[1,2])`, as well
as a symmetric matrix with a nonpositive determinant. The author tests check
the stated cases; inspect the rendered question before publication.

## PythonChecker API and a scalar example

Use `PythonChecker` when the built-in tests do not express the condition. Save
a Python file beside your question materials, register a named function in
its `CHECKERS` dictionary, then give Quarto that **filename** in
`#| python-checkers:`. Quarto reads the file when it builds the page and
includes its source for browser grading; the XML only names the function.
The [positive-multiple example](../examples.qmd#custom-python-checker) checks any
positive integer multiple of a given number. Its author module contains:

```python
def positive_multiple(student, teacher):
    if student.is_Integer is not True:
        return {"valid": False, "correct": False,
                "feedback": "Enter an integer value."}
    return bool(student > 0 and student % teacher == 0)

CHECKERS = {"positive_multiple": positive_multiple}
```

The XML names the checker and passes the learner input and teacher value:

```xml
<answertest>PythonChecker</answertest>
<sans>ans</sans>
<tans>d</tans>
<testoptions>positive_multiple</testoptions>
```

Select the module on the Quarto question block as well:

```{.stack-question #docs-custom-multiple}
#| file: ../questions/python-checker.xml
#| question: A positive integer multiple (PythonChecker)
#| python-checkers: ../questions/checkers.py
#| variants: 3
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

Both filenames in this block are relative to this `.qmd` page. For the CLI,
filenames are relative to the working directory. There is no separate source
configuration to maintain. `sans` must directly name
an input. `tans` can be a parsed teacher answer or author value, such as the
divisor `d`; `testoptions` names one entry in `CHECKERS`. It is a single
case-sensitive ASCII identifier of at most 64 characters, beginning with a letter
and followed by letters, digits, or underscores. It is not a file path or a
Python expression. The selected module is author code packaged with the page;
use only code you trust and expect learners to be able to see in a published
site.

### Callable and values

Each registered function must be callable with the two positional arguments
`student` and `teacher`, and finish synchronously. They are parsed values, not
raw answer strings. The function receives the submitted answer and whatever
teacher value the PRT's `tans` selects. This could be an expected Boolean for
a property question or a reference matrix for a different task. The API does
not pass a context object, question state or separate configuration argument.
Scalar expressions are SymPy expressions; matrices are
immutable SymPy matrices. Lists and finite sets are distinct `ListValue` and
`SetValue` objects with ordered `.args` (a set retains its submitted entries).
Equations have two `.args`; held logic has `.operator` and `.operands`;
logical constants use SymPy `true` and `false`. The collection and logic types
and `collection_items` are available from `stack_sympy.checker_api`.
These values do not promise to retain the learner's exact written arithmetic
form. A custom checker decides its own mathematical domain, within the
existing input and parser limits.

Return a Python `bool` for an ordinary true/false decision, or a dictionary:

```python
{"valid": True, "correct": False, "feedback": "Try another value."}
```

Both required fields must be Python booleans. Use `valid=False` for a response
outside this checker's domain: the learner sees an invalid-input diagnostic
and the PRT's false branch does not run. Use `valid=True, correct=False` for
a mathematically wrong response within the domain. `feedback` is optional
plain text of at most 4,096 characters. A checker cannot return a score or an
answer note; the PRT branches control those. Exceptions and malformed results
are authoring errors, rather than wrong student answers.

For a matrix, a valid result may also include one diagnostic axis:

```python
{"valid": True, "correct": False,
 "assessment": {"columns": ["correct", "dependent"]}}
```

Choose exactly `rows` or `columns`, with one status per submitted vector.
Statuses are `correct`, `incorrect`, or `dependent`. They color the editor but
do not award marks. A checker may omit the assessment entirely. If several
visited PRT nodes supply an assessment for one input, the last one displayed
wins. A quiet PRT node suppresses its checker diagnostic and assessment. The result
cannot include extra keys, an assessment for an invalid response, or a
SymPy Boolean in place of a Python `bool`.

### Test and publish

Run authored tests with the same module you render:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=_extensions/stack-sympy python -m stack_sympy.cli test \
  --file questions/python-checker.xml --python-checkers questions/checkers.py
```

The build checks referenced names, function signatures and model-answer
grading on each rendered variant. Add qtests for alternative correct answers, wrong
answers, and important PRT branches. **Validate answers** checks syntax and
input rules; the custom predicate runs on **Check answer**. The page includes
the selected Python source so the same checker runs in local tests and the
learner's browser. Keep secrets out of the module, use available Python and
SymPy features, and avoid local imports or services that the browser cannot
provide. Make checker functions deterministic; do not rely on module state
persisting from one check, variant or test to the next. Custom code can perform
arbitrary computation, so review it before
publishing. The API does not install packages or add new input types. For code
that imports questions directly, `import_xml(xml_path, python_checkers=module_path)`
selects the source; call `stack_sympy.checkers.preflight(question, variants)`
before publication to run the same author checks. `grade()` and
`run_question_tests()` execute the selected predicate on visited PRT nodes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Technical limits

A module may register at most 32 named functions in `CHECKERS`. Its source
must be a nonempty UTF-8 file no larger than 64 KiB. Feedback is plain text
up to 4,096 characters. Custom execution does not gain a server process or
additional package installation; apply a process timeout to local test runs
if authored code could take a long time.
:::
